title: W-ISA: Transactional Execution of Weight-Space Intervention Programs
domain: interpretability / model-editing infrastructure (runtime for applying weight interventions)
tasks_benchmarks: handwritten formal/casual prompt fixture (12 held-out prompts)
rank-one materialization vs PyTorch hook timing (45 timed requests)

headline_result.text: Materialized rank-one weight updates and an equivalent PyTorch hook gave identical greedy outputs on Qwen2.5-1.5B (max prompt-logit difference 0.000184), and the combined SmolLM head-ablation plus MLP projection raised WikiText-2 perplexity from 22.2353 to 22.3188 (+0.3754%).
headline_result.quote: In 45 timed requests, both intervention implementations produce identical greedy sequences at 32, 128, and 512 tokens; their maximum prompt-logit difference is 0.000184.

evidence_quality.n_runs_or_seeds: 5 timed repetitions per mode/length (deterministic greedy); single run for other experiments

key_claims.claim: W-ISA is an instruction set and transactional runtime that applies weight-space intervention programs within request scopes and restores the saved parameters afterwards.
key_claims.quote: We present W-ISA, a software instruction set and transactional runtime for executing weight- space intervention programs on pretrained language models.

key_claims.claim: The author adopts the MIT weight-space programming framing as conceptual motivation but contributes only the execution layer for supplied interventions, not an LLM that designs edits.
key_claims.quote: We adopt their weight-space programming perspective as a conceptual foundation. W-ISA’s contribution is a structured instruction and transactional execution layer for supplied interventions.

key_claims.claim: Restoration relies on saved byte-exact snapshots, not on numerically inverting the edit; undo and replay matched across two separately launched processes.
key_claims.quote: Undo restored the original weights and recorded outputs; replay restored the edited state. Two sepa- rately launched processes matched in saved logits, token sequences, direction values, and parameter digests.

key_claims.claim: An activation-triggered conditional rule fired on 4 of 6 held-out matched prompts with no false positives (balanced accuracy 0.833), and all twelve conditional requests kept their original greedy outputs.
key_claims.quote: All twelve conditional requests retained their original greedy token se- quences.

key_claims.claim: Materializing the weight update costs extra time-to-first-token and memory compared with a forward hook (e.g., median TTFT 166.4 ms vs 51.1 ms at 512 tokens; ~499 MiB RSS increase vs ~1.6 MiB).
key_claims.quote: The measured W-ISA application medians are 48.866, 56.059 and 115.142 ms for the three length groups; restoration medians are 2.500, 2.413 and 2.624 ms.

limitations_stated.text: The shared model lock serializes requests for the lifetime of an intervention, so concurrent requests do not run in parallel.
limitations_stated.quote: The shared model lock serializes participating requests for the lifetime of the intervention.

limitations_stated.text: Snapshots cover the full target parameter even when only a slice is edited, which drives memory cost.
limitations_stated.quote: Snapshots cover full target parameters, including when an instruction selects a smaller slice.

notes_for_review: This is an engineering runtime for applying hand-specified weight edits (ablation, projection, rank-one) with exact restoration; no LLM reads or writes weights, so it is WSP only in framing. Evidence is correctness and timing checks on two small models with deterministic greedy decoding; the steering effect itself is tiny (3 of 12 responses changed, perplexity change under 0.4%). The code is described as MIT-licensed but no repository link is given in the text.
